There is quite a lot of love put into this game and you can see how passionate the devs were. An incredible experience I definitely recommend jrpg fans to experience themselves. 
To start I'll say that the OST is stellar and there are so many great memorable tracks, definitely going to listen to a playlist of the OST later to pick out my favorites. Graphics are great but more importantly the art direction is incredible, between unique enemy design, beautiful and huge areas that are each so good you can't help by take screenshots and many unique yet cohesive themes to everything. Going through the world map is quite the experience. Game also has some really nice qol/ it's own take on some usual jrpg mechanics like consumable or save/checkpoints. Also enabling faster travel method early is a godsend. I do feel like you could unlock some earlier but not much to complain there.or the 2 most important aspects of the game I do feel like while both were great but there's definitely room for imporvement.

For the gameplay I really thought I'll dislike parry/dodge centric turn based combat. not because I don't like parries since both Sekiro and Nine Sols are two of my favorite games of all time and both are heavily parry based, but because I thought having parries instead of defense and having interaction with enemy be based on parrying/dodging will diminish much of the in combat strategic thinking that I like so much about turn based combat... and it honestly kinda does but the game is fairly balanced that both parries can elevate you/help you punch above your weight but don't overturn build making and changing up stuff to fit enemies and the game is fun to play... up to a certain point.Don't get me wrong game was still quite fun but as I was doing well balancing both aspect I realized at some point midway through act 2 after doing a lot of optional stuff I started melting enemies and bosses alike with my more optimized builds. Some major bosses barely got to attack more than twice. I know changing from normal to expert will likely make those bosses not die as quickly(and I intend to either switch to expert for post game stuff or do another run on expert in the future) but then I would feel like the pendulum will swing heavily into making the game rely too much on parries like I feared. I really wish this game had no parry/dodge system since the customization is great but the interactivity with my enemy feels minimal, kinda like playing yugioh I am just going through the motions of my gameplan with little regard to what my enemy is doing and the only thing the enemy can really do is just attack me multiple times.

As for the story. Overall narrative is great, I do think some of the themes weren't as well executed(but can't really talk about that without spoiling) but I was always interested in seeing what's going to happen next and the way it was presented moved me multiple times, this aspect really shined during act 2 and 3. The main cast were all very likeable, the side characters were good and the villains all were really interesting to explore. Banter around the party was great and fireplace scenes added some much needed interaction between party members and here's where I pivot into some criticism that I don't think the cast really talked as much as I expected them to, especially during dungeons/areas, much beyond commenting on what's currently going on in the area and I think the game should have had more dialogue. Certain characters had some great development, some felt neglected even when the story tried to give them their "moment". The social link like system felt very out of place despite some scenes being necessary(and would have been better if those were just campfire interactions or during the actual dungeon/area progression) and sometimes didn't even make sense to happen when they did. And I feel like the path the cast needed to take was relatively guided and never felt without a next destination or with a need to think what to do next. I also wanted certain aspects about the world/certain characters motivations be explored a lot more and I feel like they never will be and exploring those more might expose more flaws.

Really hard to talk about the game while being vague but I do really recommend it to anyone. Despite some faults I still loved the game and it is probably going to be top 20 if not top 10. Would score it around 9.3/10.

I’ve been playing games for most of my life. I love difficult games, complicated systems, bosses that make you question your life choices, and achievements that turn “just one more try” into 5 AM.

I just finished Expedition 33 with almost every achievement unlocked, and I can say this without hesitation: this is one of the best games I have ever played.

The soundtrack alone deserves an award. There are games with good music, games with great music, and then there are games where you stop what you’re doing just to listen. Expedition 33 belongs to the last category. The music doesn’t simply accompany the game — it becomes part of its identity. Even after finishing it, some tracks are still playing in my head.

The story is another huge highlight. It is unusual, unpredictable, emotional, and refreshingly unwilling to follow the most obvious path. I spent a lot of time trying to guess where things were going, and the game repeatedly reminded me that I wasn’t nearly as clever as I thought I was. No spoilers — just know that it rewards paying attention.

The characters feel like actual people rather than quest dispensers with tragic backstories attached. They have personalities, flaws, chemistry, humor, and believable relationships with each other. By the end of the game, I genuinely cared about this group.

And then there is the combat and progression system.

This is where the hardcore-player part of my brain became extremely happy.

There are plenty of ways to build your characters, experiment with different combinations, optimize your setup, abuse synergies, completely rethink a build, and then discover something even more ridiculous twenty minutes later. Progression feels meaningful rather than being just “number goes up.” The game constantly gives you new toys and encourages you to figure out how badly you can break them.

The combat itself manages to make turn-based battles feel active and intense. When everything clicks — your build works, your timing is right, and you execute a difficult fight almost perfectly — it feels fantastic.

And yes, some encounters can absolutely destroy you.

Good.

I wouldn’t have wanted it any other way.

What impressed me most is how complete the whole experience feels. Great combat alone would have been enough. A great story alone would have been enough. Great characters or an incredible soundtrack would have been enough.

Expedition 33 somehow has all of them.

I started playing because the game looked interesting.

I finished it hunting almost every achievement, listening to the soundtrack outside the game, and wondering what exactly I’m supposed to play after this.

That might be the biggest problem with Expedition 33:

It makes other games (especially the new ones from the big studios) feel worse.

I didn't get into this game right away. Actually the first I'd heard of it was at the game awards, and like most people I was really perplexed as to why it was winning EVERYTHING. Sure it looked like it had a really good cast with Charlie Cox and Ben Starr, but I had it in my head that the game was going to be French Arthouse, have a story that was really obtuse like some of the Final Fantasy games. I got this game a few months back, didn't touch it. It was actually my dissatisfaction with Star Wars Zero Company that made me finally try this out only two weeks ago and... My god it deserved absolutely deserves all of those awards.

I don't know what the narrative was about with this game being an industry plant, as from what I know it was a former ubisoft employee that went to make their own studio. There is no way in hell this was an industry plant from Ubisoft they have NEVER cooked something anywhere near this game imo. This game is a love letter to RPGs, Belle Epoque France, incredible character writing, fantastic visuals, and really sick ass music. I'll just say right here this game is a 10/10. It's a game that I think everyone should play. I have some a few nitpicks, but these don't bring it down from being a 10.

The Positives:

This is (near) perfect turn-based combat. The developers took systems from almost every RPG and put them together perfectly, and it all comes down to one very good decision on the developers part: AP. In most RPGs you have mana, a resource that starts full after being healed but goes down the more you use it for spells and ♥♥♥♥. In Clair Obscur its the opposite: your AP starts low, and you have to do actions to build it. Thankfully you have so many different ways to build AP across characters, and very unique ways to use it throughout the entire game. As for defense, you have the universal options of dodging (which has a longer invulnerability window and less recovery time) or parrying (which has a tighter window, can't be spammed as easily, but rewards you with 1 AP per parry AND if you parry all hits of a sequence you get a counterattack). I could go on forever about the other parts of combat, but I think it's better for the player to experience it firsthand. You always feel like you have something to do in battles, and I don't think I've ever run from a battle out of boredom.

The plot is a breath of fresh air for RPGs. I won't give away a lot here, but the premise is that every year a being called the Paintress wipes away a number on a monolith counting down and writes the next number down. Whoever is over that number age wise evaporates into petals. It reminded of Logan's Run, if the population in Logan's Run actually wanted to stop the age limit the whole time. What I really like about the story is that the twists and plot beats are very much earned. Everyone in your party feels like their own living breathing character, and you really get to know them. That's all I feel like I should say on that, because I don't want to spoil anything.

The music I think is the most underated aspect of this game. Many, many great tracks in this game that range from haunting, to intense, to legitimate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ jams. It's a phenominal soundtrack and just another part of what makes this game perfect.

Graphical optimization also felt perfect for it. I came off from Zero Company looking very blocky due to it's optimization, but Clair looks ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing even on medium settings. It never chugged for me, always looked amazing, and to my knowledge never dipped below 60 fps outside maybe one cutscene. I'm on a Nvidia 3070 (or 3060 I don't remember) and it runs fantastic.

Lastly, the meat of the game. I went into this expecting a 20 or 30 hour game... no. I'm 64 hours in and I still haven't done everything I've wanted on my first playthrough. There is so much to customize and experiment with in this game, both in terms of costumes and combat that I've never once felt bored. I usually don't replay games, especially long RPGs like this... but I think I'll at least try a New Game Plus mode if that's a thing with how much there is to use. Alright with all of that out of the way, lets get to-

The (very few) Negatives:

For an RPG that's clearly well-versed in the all time greats (Thousand Year Door, Chrono Trigger, Persona 5) and goes out of its way to use its combat systems to the fullest, there are some headscratching choices they made here and there. 

The one big flaw in the combat system is that you can't switch party members mid fight. You get to use your reserve members if the first wave get KO'd, but you can't actively swap them out like a lot of turn based RPGs. This matters particularly if your character is using a certain element type on their weapon, and the enemy is immune to that type entirely. At best it makes a fight more obnoxious than it should be, and at worst it forces you to abandon and go back to the nearest save point to reformat your party.

The second big issue is that if you retry a fight and it has a cutscene before it... it reloads the cutscene and you gotta skip it all over again. Maybe the cutscenes mask loading the fight? But I doubt it given how fast it goes into it when you skip the cutscene.

Some other minor nitpicks. There's no minimap whatsoever. There's an overworld map, that is a good map imo, but no dungeon maps. I think for the most part... this is fine. The dungeons have a lot of different side paths, but they're designed in a way that you don't really get lost most of the time. There's a few places I definitely would've preferred a minimap though, so I wish that had been a togglable option.

Lastly, I've heard some reviewers mention that doing side content first makes main story fights very easy. I didn't feel like this was the case, but I was also playing on the hardest difficulty. I honestly feel like the hardest difficulty should be the go-to for playing the game, as it really challenges you to optimize your offense and defense. There is a 9,999 damage cap for much of the game, and this does keep you from beating some side bosses in the middle of the game. I wonder if the lower difficulty options allowed the reviewers to beat bosses they really shouldn't have and given them a drastic amount of levels.

Anyways, 10/10 game. Deserved every award it got.

I don't know what I expected and I'm still disappointed.
For all this time I dodged every single piece of media to not get spoiled in the slightest. I wanted to see why this game triumphed over some of my favorite games when it comes to reviews and other accolades.

But here I am.
This "game" consists of essentially 60% cutscenes, 30% of running around in forked linear level design and 10% of combat.

Cutscenes and story has been alright so far, even though I don't understand most of it. It's just pulling more and more high fantasy story elements out of its butt until it gets so convoluted that the main motivator for keeping up with the story is getting answers to your questions.
It's not exactly piquing my interest if I am thrown into a world where nothing makes sense from the start. Worldbuilding bloat that keeps adding entities, systems, dimensions until I, as a player, lose the grounding in the setting and lose my interest in the characters because the only (!) thing that connects me and the protagonists is that they are humanoid. I don't even know if they are humans at this point. 

Exploration is mostly sprinting through the level and collecting every glowing item until eventually a cutscene triggers after some boundary. It looks great, I'll give them that. But it feels like a cheap "look how pretty it is... don't worry about the gameplay, look at the flowers!".
There's also a lot of environmental incoherence when the setting communicates me a destroyed otherworldly level but every other section has platforming parkours with 5 perfectly spaced apart surfaces for you to jump on like God himself built them for you to hike up this small cliff to find this one small upgrade. Or these pitons in cliffs for you to climb on by literally holding the stick forward the entire time. Who genuinely likes these parts? Who feels engaged by platforming in a AAA game that is not centered around it?

And then there's the combat, oh boy. 
I, for one, like methodical turn-based combat. It gives me the freedom to plan ahead and find synergies between my characters. Or maybe make glass-cannon builds, both can be fun. 
But most of it goes out the window when the game gives you the option to perfect-parry attacks that reward you not only with more AP but also with a counter that can absolutely wreck most enemies like a full attack.
Also, I am a big fan of the Souls series, and especially Sekiro.
But who in their right mind thought it would be a good idea to combine the two?

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was an interesting experience to finish, but after completing the game, I can’t say I would recommend buying it at full price. Maybe for a few dollars or euros on a deep sale, but there are simply too many much better-developed RPGs and JRPGs available.

The music was easily the strongest part of the game for me. I genuinely loved the soundtrack. It does a great job of creating atmosphere and supporting both the quieter moments and the more dramatic scenes. It’s probably the part of the game I’ll remember the most.

The story didn’t really work for me. By around the middle of the first act, the direction it was heading in had already become fairly obvious, which made most of the later revelations much less impactful. I kept expecting the narrative to introduce something that would significantly change my perception of what was happening, but that never really happened. I also found some of the conflicts and contradictions in the characters’ motivations more off-putting than compelling. Instead of making them feel more complex or human, these moments often made their actions and decisions harder for me to connect with. Character development in general felt limited, which was particularly disappointing for a game that places so much emphasis on its narrative and cast.

The gameplay is enjoyable at first, but as an RPG it lacks depth. Most of the systems are straightforward, and there isn’t much need to carefully think about your build or experiment with different approaches. Once you understand the basic mechanics, the effective choices become fairly obvious. Build variety also feels quite limited for the genre. I would have liked to see more meaningful trade-offs, stronger specialization, and more viable ways to build and play each character.

The world itself is good. I liked the overall art direction, environment design, monster design, and character design. Visually, the game has a distinctive identity and there are plenty of locations that are enjoyable to explore. The presentation is clearly one of the game’s stronger aspects.

Overall, I finished the game, but I wouldn’t recommend buying it at anything close to full price. Perhaps it’s worth picking up for a few euros during a deep sale. There are many RPGs and JRPGs on the market with deeper gameplay systems, more interesting build variety, stronger character development, and more engaging stories.

Considering all of that, I don’t really understand the extraordinary level of praise Expedition 33 received or why it ended up being regarded as Game of the Year. The music and presentation are excellent, and I can understand why those aspects resonated with so many people, but for me they weren’t enough to compensate for the shallow RPG mechanics, predictable narrative, and characters I found difficult to connect with.

I bought the game after the “game award incident,” not knowing much about it other than it being a JRPG with a cool looking UI. The game starts off heavily narrative driven, but still gives you the option to learn the base mechanics before throwing you into the ordeal. The thing you instantly notice is the melancholic, operatic soundtrack that sets the tone going forward. The start of Act I already shows off the game's great environmental design and use of colours, which the game keeps up until the end. The characters fit nicely into this world visually speaking, even if the monologues and dialogue might be a little cheesy at times.

The gameplay itself is somewhat interesting, the need to adapt and build synergy between the characters keeps the repetitive gameplay loop bearable. Enemy encounters are usually very similar or identical, even among different enemy groups. The battles themselves are enjoyable, as you need to be accurate with your timings while attacking, dodging, and parrying. Overall, the system repeats itself heavily, which becomes painfully evident in Act II. The story is still there, but it’s basically just a copy and paste of Act I, minus the new scenery.

One thing we also “get to have” whilst progressing through the game is new companions with their own abilities and powers. While it’s great to give the player more options to “choose” from, the game doesn't actually let you choose much. Instead, when your main trio gets wiped out along with all their synergy, you’re left with Team Bravo, AKA the two outcasts you haven't spent much time with and their total lack of synergy.

Now, what actually made me write this review was Act III. It's always nice to see different media “risk it for the biscuit,” so to speak. The music, enemies, environment, atmosphere, characters, monologues, dialogue, and THE story all get a huge buff here... without spoiling anything specific. This game is definitely worth looking into, even with its faults it is easily one of “the games”.

The real star though is the combat. It’s turn-based so you can plan out your skills, but you can’t just put the controller down. You have to actively nail timed attacks, and dodging or parrying enemy swings in real time makes fights feel super tense. I've played a lot of games that deal with loss. Most of them tell you about it. 
This one makes you feel it in your chest.

[b]MAJOR SPOILERS WARNING[/b]

On the surface it looks like a gorgeous game about stopping an apocalypse. But underneath that it's a story about a mother who couldn't let go of her dead son, a father destroying an entire world to save his wife from herself, and a daughter caught between two lives wondering which one is actually hers. Nobody here is a villain. Everyone is just broken in their own way and trying to survive it.

Then there's Verso. A painted copy of a dead boy, fully aware that he is not real. He never asked to exist. He just woke up one day inside someone else's pain and had to figure out what to do with that. He spends decades watching people die, loses the person he loved, grows tired of everything, and eventually decides the kindest thing he can do is end it all. Not out of hatred. Out of pure exhaustion. And his own mother, when she finally sees him, looks him in the eyes and says: [i]you are not my Verso.[/i] After a century of feeling and losing and carrying all of it. Still just a copy.

And somewhere in the canvas a faceless little boy wanders alone, painting endlessly, keeping the whole world alive. Everyone made decisions around him, about him, for him. The only one who ever bothered to ask what he wanted was Verso himself.

The game never lets you feel comfortable. It builds people you care about and then asks you to decide their fate. Do you save a painted world full of people who laugh, love and die just like anyone else? Or do you free a soul that has been trapped inside it since the day he died?

Neither answer is clean. The game doesn't pretend otherwise.

[i]Life keeps forcing cruel choices.[/i] No other game has made me feel the weight of that sentence the way this one did.

[b]See things as they are, not how you want them to be.[/b]

I give most games a very fair chance and I heard nothing except great reviews about 33, but I simply cannot recommend this game.

There are a few real simple reasons as to why I'm just completely unimpressed by it.

#1 - The voice acting is unfitting to the characters (somewhat) and it feels like it's almost robotic. Not in the terms of "AI", but the casting and the voice direction must have been off and it definitely shows.

#2 - The graphics, run animations, battle sequences, it all feels very Xbox 360 era and not in a good way. I felt like I was playing a tech demo of a game that had too much saturation, too much bloom, too much in the way of an identity crisis. The scenery was fighting to find itself (steampunk, fantasy, classic Victorian, 70's British, etc) and I just couldn't get behind the semi-weird cartoony nature in an otherwise random universe.

#3 - It tosses you into the game and tries to impress on you the seriousness of the story right away, without really giving you time to develop a character, grasp the situation or even understand much else. The movement was weird as well; switching quickly between a low-tech adventure platformer (felt like Wolverine honestly) and a turn based combat system (almost similar to FF13, which was weird). I see what they were going for and it's an easy game to understand gameplay wise, but it's tossed at you as if this was a sequel or you were meant to be at least an hour into the game prior to everything being dropped.

Honestly I can't quite put my finger on why I dislike this game overall aside from saying a massive TL;DR.

TL;DR - The game has a definite identity crisis, the graphics are weird, the voice acting is weird, there was definitely AI used in this (undisclosed), the music is good but not fitting to the situations (bad tact/context) and it just overall felt like a weird tech demo. If you like old school RPGs with fun concepts, go find a way to play Lost Odyssey or Legend of Dragoon. If you want a very stylized RPG with great characters and a modern style, check out BG3 or for the cartoony-side try DQ11's super ultra turbo edition.

But this game? It just feels... unpolished.

Gameplay: 18.5/20
Combining the traditional static turn-based strategies of a JRPG with a motion-based parry/dodge system of an action game, this game fits in a comfortable middle ground. 
Graphic/Art Style: 10/10
Truly a unique art style with elements from Baroque, Neo-classical, and Victorian era styles. 
Content/Pacing: 17.5/20
The amount of content is sufficient for a 60-80 hrs experience (I managed to 100% all the achievements after 190hrs but I'm sure better players could 100% the game in a fraction of the time). My one criticism in this area is toward the end of Act 3 with all the world map opened up, my characters became too strong and overleveled after completing most of the side areas. The final story boss fight became an anticlimactic joke (this is despite playing on Expert). 
The game loot works fine for the most part in encouraging exploration of the open-world map to get better gear. 
Optimized performance: 18/20
Not much issue with performance although I am running on a rig with NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070. The biggest issue is with the aggressive shadow and light/dark contrast (some of the areas are either too dark or too bright).

One of the best game I ever saw and played. Expedition 33 was actually the first game I played on computer. Before that, I used to mostly play nintendo games, or watch a lot of gameplays, thinking I didnt really need to play a game if I could watch it. 
While that is partially true (watching a youtuber you like play a game can also be pretty cool), playing it really made me realize what I was missing out.


POSITIVES

GRAPHICS

First of, and obviously, the graphics are phenomenal, there are a lot of worlds and areas to visit that each have their own beautiful concept and are visually crazy to look at! Each time I entered a new place I couldnt help but let out a 'wow!' each time and take pictures. (personal favorite, the Visages island :) )
And thats only talking about the landscapes, the characters are also all very well made, and even more the creatures and enemies that have amazing looks, some look enchanting, some scary, cute and so on, and there are tons of them!
The acting is also very human and doesnt feel at all awkward. You can notice small stuff the characters does when they aren nervous for exemple, which I really love and really makes them have their own charming personalities. I easily grew emotionally connected to the characters very quickly because of that!


MUSIC

And of course the soundtracks, more than a hundred in this game, and most are in my playlist, and most I remember the exact scene the song was played, which I rarely do when I do not find the music memorable. I usually had to pause the battle simply for listening to the music.


GAMEPLAY

As for the game mechanics, I have no issues with and found it really fun. I did hear a lot of people where hesitant to start because it was a turn based game. Do not worry, this game can really get really hard and I hardly even consider it turn base game! During the battles you will be met for exemple the dodge and parry system, so even when its not your turn you will have to learn the moves of the enemies if you want to take less damage and not die. I also liked how many diversity there was in the enemies attacks, most have their own set of attacks that can go of a single one, or some enemies with more than 10 different, which can usually be very hard usually when the enemy has multiple phases!
Its also really cool how you can manage your team, and how all characters have different ways of attacks. Pictos and Luminas are also pretty fun to look into what buffs and combos with them you can make to make your team crazy strong.


STORY  (no spoil)

I honestly didnt think at the story would be this amazing. But lets say in the two hour mark you start it, you will immediatly understand that this story is a lot more complicated than you originally thought. For 40h of story, you will keep asking yourself questions and will  leave you confused for the most game, which is to me what I like the most. I always love to make little theories and try to understand with thr clues we are being given slowly throughout the story, and surprisingly still be shocked by the turn the game took. And I was even more surprised that the story, with how complexe it was, was still completely understandable at the end. And even better when you replay it or watch others play it, understand what you didnt understand in your first playthrough. It was to me a very beautiful, tragic journey I followed with all these amazing characters


STORY (spoil)

I have thoughts on the ending. Massive spoilers:

[spoiler] I greatly appreciate that, during a time when it feels like any ending that isn’t unanimously positive and happy, Expedition 33 takes a different approach. At the end of the game, you get to choose between two endings. One ending forces the characters to face a somber reality while the other one grants the characters what they think is going to be happily ever after. 

If you choose to give them happily ever after, you’re shown an ending where sacrifices that are temporary and happiness that is eternal is nothing more than a naïve fantasy.

The other ending puts in your hands the ability to cut down that fantasy narrative and make them face reality, even when the other characters do not want to. 

I found this especially moving because after numerous brain surgeries, I was put on very powerful steroids to help me heal. They caused me to go psychotic, and I experienced wild hallucinations for a month that elevated me and my place in the world to a fantastical high. When I came down from that high, I had to face the reality that I was not in any way an auspicious or noteworthy person. I am, in fact, disabled. 

This is the same struggle that the character who wants a happily ever after goes through. In reality, she is not the hero of a fantasy adventure, she is a grief stricken and disabled woman living a sheltered life where she is overlooked at best and despised at worst. 

This game gave me a sword and told me I could live in the fantasy as long as I wanted, or I could cut down the fantasy at the expense of facing my own unremarkable true nature and disabled body. I am very thankful for that. Because that choice is something that I make every day when I get up out of bed to face the day. [/spoiler]

Posting this review on behalf of my husband, who played Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 through Family Sharing. I’ve also played and finished the game myself, and absolutely loved it, so I can definitely understand where he’s coming from with this one. 😆

The following is his review:
Yes, the game was heavily hyped when it released, but having pretty much finished the game, minus some secret bosses, I can 100% say with certainty that the game deserves all the acclaim it has gotten.

The biggest thing about the game, is the combat system. Yes, it is a turn-based combat system, but in actual practice, some of the fights in the game barely feels like turn-based at all. This is because of the parry and dodge mechanic that are integral to the combat system, in particular parrying. It is hard to describe how amazing the parry in this game feels, only that it feels AMAZING when you land them and then with the follow up counter. I don't recall any games in my memory that gives me the same satisfaction as counter attacks do in this game.

Then, there's the music in the game. I don't typically take note of in-game music, but if I were to describe the music in this game in one word, it will be "phenomenal". And I'd like to think that the music played a very significant part in how well-received the game was. And almost each of the music tells a story, if you are interested in them. There are hauntingly beaufitul song pieces, hype battle music, relaxing background music, all of which lends itself to creating a very memorable experience.

And lastly, the story. The game explores a very interesting element and it was masterfully written, with compelling characters. The game is so easily spoilable, that writing about the story is a very difficult thing. So I will just end that the story of the game is fantastic.

Overall, having played through the entirety of the game, I believe the hype surrounding the game, was entirely justified. I am very much looking forward to what Sandfall Interactive will cook up in the future.

I start Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 knowing one thing:
this world is already counting my days.

Every year, the Paintress wakes up, writes a number, and everyone older than that number simply disappears.
No boss fight.
No last words.
Just erased — politely, artistically, and brutally.

You don’t play as a chosen one.
You play as someone already scheduled to die.
Expedition 33 isn’t about saving the world — it’s about walking forward anyway, fully aware that time is winning.

The combat is turn-based, but it refuses to feel safe.
Timing matters.
Dodging matters.
Every action feels like the game asking, “Are you sure this is how you want to spend this moment?”

The world is haunting.
Beautiful in a way that hurts.
Surreal cities, broken landscapes, and silence that feels heavier than dialogue.
Even when nothing attacks you, the atmosphere does.

And the characters…
They don’t speak like heroes.
They speak like people who know the ending and still choose to move.
There’s hope here — but it’s quiet, fragile, and constantly under threat.

• Joined the expedition → Accepted my expiration date.
• Fought beautifully → Still felt small.
• Kept moving forward → Because stopping doesn’t change the number.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is art + inevitability + quiet defiance.
If you love this game… congratulations, you’re comfortable staring mortality in the face and pressing “continue.”

This game wrecked me in the best way possible.I sank 61 hours into it over the months, started back in May, and finally hit “The End” on September 12. Went from the first steps in Lumière all the way through Spring Meadows, Flying Waters, Ancient Sanctuary, Gestral Village, Esquie’s Nest, Stone Wave Cliffs, Forgotten Battlefield, Monoco’s Station, Old Lumière, both Axons, the Monolith, beating the Paintress, and returning home. Unlocked every party member, maxed relationships with Sciel and Esquie, learned all of Esquie’s abilities, and knocked out a bunch of the combat-focused achievements (Overcharge Breaks, Perfect Flow with Lune, Synergy with Maelle, Maximisation with Sciel, Rank S with Verso, Wheel Control with Monoco, etc.). Still missing some of the heavier completionist stuff like all journals, all music records, fully upgrading a weapon, level 66/99, and the no-damage boss challenges — but the main journey is done.The story hits hard. That whole setup with the Paintress painting a number every year and people past that age just… vanishing is simple, bleak, and incredibly effective. The characters feel real, the voice acting is excellent, and the writing balances melancholy, wonder, and the occasional dark humor perfectly. The Belle Époque-inspired world is gorgeous — dreamy, painterly, and full of atmosphere. Combat is the real star though: turn-based with real-time timing elements that keep every fight engaging. Building around each character’s unique mechanics is super satisfying, and the bosses (especially the Axons and the Paintress) feel like proper tests.It’s not perfect. It’s more linear than a lot of big RPGs, and once you finish the main story there’s still a chunk of side content and mastery left if you want 100%. But for a debut from a small studio, this is an absolute triumph. The presentation, music, combat, and emotional payoff are all top-tier.If you like stylish, story-driven RPGs with actual mechanical depth in the battles, just play it. 61 hours well spent and I’m still thinking about it. Highly recommended.

[h1][b] TLDR: Stunning art, incredible music, and a brilliant turn-based combat system make this an easy recommendation and an absolute must play. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Music
➕Graphics
➕Intriging plot
➕Turned based combat + Dark Souls mechanics work very well
➕Lots of optional (often incredibly difficult) content
➕Good build potential

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Animations, especially in cutscenes, appear a bit stiff (Unreal Engine issue)
➖Some audio bugs in battle with crackling music
➖Menu sorting, like by level or power,  is never saved between sessions. Menu sorting also lacks options like sorting Monoco’s dozens of skills by type (mask color) 

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [10/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world is exquisitely created. Not only is it a sight to behold, like a living painting, but it is created well for gameplay elements like traversal and minigames. There is a wide variety of different biomes consisting of beaches, snow, and many that don’t fit into a classification due to being of more abstract nature. 
The areas are mostly linear with some side paths that usually involve a fight and a treasure item - currency/gear. 
I would say the game world is amazing and a huge part of what makes the game so special. 

The narrative is super intriguing, but doesn’t finish as strong. At the start of the game, you set out on expedition #33. There is something called a “Gommage” where everyone who is of age or older are “Thanos snapped” out of existence. So the people who are going to disappear during the next Gommage set out on an expedition to try to put an end to all the death. 
When arriving at the expedition landing point, it’s like you’re walking across decades of lore and the result of failed attempts that push only slightly further to make way for the next expedition. It’s grim, it’s dark, and yet hauntingly beautiful. 
I was immersed right from the get-go and while the plot didn’t end as strong as it started, it kept me interested throughout. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [9/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop consists of going to a designated area, fighting your way through enemies via turn-based battles, and eventually ending on a boss fight with long cutscenes sprinkled in between. 
This being a turned-based RPG truly sets the bar for the potential of turn-based games. The combat flawlessly weaves in dodges and parries into the combat that turns the combat into a fast-paced and insanely engaging difference from other turn-based games like Final Fantasy. 
The game's progression system is interesting in that it’s deceptively simple, yet opens up as the game advances. Instead of a large amount of gear, you get a weapon and 3 “Picto” slots, which are basically accessory slots that give passive abilities. The catch is that you can unlock those Picto abilities to equip on any character by using points they get when leveling up. It reminds me of Final Fantasy 9 how you use a piece of gear in enough battles and you can unlock the passive abilities to equip without the gear (just on any character here). The equipped Pictos combined with the weapon passive combined with character skills, of which you can have 6, allows some fairly intricate build potential, especially as you progress in the game and unlock some crazier abilities. 

The difficulty is good. I played on Normal difficulty and was challenged, but rarely died. The game is exceptionally forgiving in allowing you to redo fights or just simply backout of fights. The game uses a lot of Dark Souls mechanics though dodges and parrying, but doesn’t actively punish you for failing, which is great for experimentation. 
However, there are optional bosses, and unless you are either insanely overleveled/optimized or a god at parrying/dodging, you’re going to constantly get 1 or 2-shot. The optional content is no joke (look up the Simon fight on Youtube). 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [10/10] [/b] [/h1]
The graphics are exceptionally good. This is easily PS5-era fidelity and beyond. The cutscenes look stellar and the area's art style is phenomenal. 
The performance was perfect. I played the game fully maxed and ran into no issues at all. 
Perhaps the only thing I can nitpick here is with the Unreal Engine making animations and movements stiff, floaty, and often going through the environment. This is a consistent thing with 3rd person UE games and it’s still noticeable here, despite the otherwise beautiful looking setting. 
I did encounter a bug that seemed to have a lot of discussion online - audio crackling during combat, which is a shame because the music is SO good. I wasn’t able to find a fix for this, despite all my other games sounding fine. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [10/10] [/b] [/h1]
I absolutely cannot stress enough how amazing the music is in this game. Simple random encounter fights have musical scores that rival end boss fights in other JRPGs. The soundtrack is so good, that I literally added multiple songs to my Spotify playlist. 
Aside from the amazing soundtrack, the voice acting is very good, a slight complaint being how there are 4x “Rough & sandpaper” voice sounding male characters. The men badly need some diversity. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There is a NG+, but due to lack of player choice and a mostly linear game, there isn’t a whole lot of replay value. 
There is a lot of optional content to do and level up, but as far as having a different experience or outcome when replaying the game, it’s not really possible outside of builds, which don’t open up fully until the endgame anyways. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [9/10] [/b] [/h1]
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 (COE33) has fully earned the award of Game of the Year 2025. I was constantly impressed, over and over again, as I played through the game. It’s truly an experience. The hardest part for me is to decide whether to rate this game a 9 or a 10. 

Let’s talk about some negatives, and there aren’t many at all. 
I mentioned above how the plot doesn’t finish as strong as it starts. Once I hit Act 3 and the big reveal presented itself, I was a bit letdown after learning that [spoiler]the entire world that the expedition takes place in isn’t really real[/spoiler]. It’s a fairly old narrative deflection and kind of made all the amazing lore in the beginning not as meaningful. But still, at that point I’m 40 hours in and no way I’m stopping. 
Other than the small narrative gripe, there’s just some other smaller things - UI sorting isn’t as good as I’d like, Unreal Engine feels like the typical crappy UE at times

The good? SO much. The game is simply phenomenal. The narrative starts out so strong that it's hard to put down. There are so many mysteries and questions that I have to know, it’s like reading a good book. 
The music is astounding. I can’t get numerous songs out of my head and they are on my Spotify list now. 
I think more than anything is that E33 shows the potential that turn-based RPGs still have. While games like Final Fantasy have moved into more action-oriented combat, E33 has taken the classic turn-based formula and just smacked on the Dark Souls mechanics to turn it into some of the most exciting combat I’ve ever played. It’s truly game changing and I hope more games follow the blueprints laid here to inject new elements into old systems. 

Overall, I fully recommend this game. I decided to give it a 9/10 due to the low replay value and the small narrative fumbling.

[h1]Yes[/h1]
$50 is worth it to me considering I played for 50+ hours. I would say that anything below $30 is a steal, but Steam’s historical low is around $40.

Expedition 33 is one of those rare games where almost everything came together for me: the world, characters, music, combat and story all feel like parts of the same thing rather than separate systems.

I expected to enjoy it, but I didn’t expect to become this attached to it. The art direction is incredible, the soundtrack stays with you long after you stop playing, and the combat manages to make a turn-based RPG feel active without losing the part I actually like about turn-based games.

But the reason I love it is the emotional side. The game is beautiful, strange and often genuinely sad without constantly trying to remind you how emotional it is. By the end I cared about the characters and the world far more than I expected to.

There are plenty of great games that I finish, appreciate and move on from. This wasn’t one of them. I still want reasons to return to it.

I played a lot of the game thus far, and I have to say, like every other review in here that is a thumbs down, I have mixed feelings about this game. It's beautiful, cinematic, colorful and flashy and dayum did they nail the face expressions in the dialogs, even the small unrelevant dialogs feel compelling because of it. And don't get me started with the music, that stuff is actually what brought me back into the game after i quit it after several hours of playtime the first time. 

But, this is a negative review, so why the high praise? Well, this isn't a game really, or to put it better, the reason this game is so well beloved is probablly not the gameplay aspect. They experimented with two aspects, pairing a classic RPG with Parry Mechanics from Soulslike games. Refreshing the classic JRPG formula is kinda neccessary to reach the broader market nowedays, and it can work, see FF7 remake with the hack and slay generic autoattacks, Undertale with their pacifist approch or Inscryption if your into some horror deckbuilding. But the parry mechanic completly removes the strategy aspect of the game. It doesn't matter how you build your characters, the parry mechanic is the one and only key to this game. Most of the game I just ignored the pictomechanics, level ups and character customization, and when I finally thought to myself that it's kinda time to take a dive into the level ups again, I barely noticed a difference. As soon as a boss just permantly removes a member from your party, should you fail to parry (you cant even revive them) you kinda feel like strategy means nothing in this game. Sure it made the boss badass, and sure you can easily learn to parry it after at most some tries, but this really shows the priorities of the game. It feels tiresome to play the game, especially if you fight the same enemies multiple times and have already mastered the parry timings, then it's just stupidly playing down the same 2 ryhtm attacks over and over again. But just like every half baked menu of the game (good luck finding where you can change the appearance of your characters, or finding out where to permantly lock in pictos) the gameplay could have cooked a bit longer. This just seems like a top-tier movie burried in a mediocre at best game. If you wish for a good parry game, play Sekiro, it's a really good game, one of the best, and it actually fits with the parry mechanic, and if your into strategy, play ANY other game. However, the twist where they added dodge and parry mechanics to this system is implemented in such a way where strategy becomes completely irrelevant and the way you build your character and execute your turns doesn't matter AT ALL as long as you can press the parry button at the right moment; missing a parry is lethal and can one shot your character, but landing one completely nullifies ANY incoming damage, and hitting the full chain of parries inflicts HUGE counter-damage. Ultimately this is a gorgeous piece of art trapped inside a miserable video game.  If you have the patience to endure endless, rhythm-game parry slogs and wander through lifeless, empty expanses just to earn the next scrap of genuinely brilliant story, you might squeeze some value out of it. I completed around 95% of optional content in the Expeditioner mode (aka normal mode). I won't be 100% it because there's just some content I do not care for. Overall, I had a great time with this game, but I do feel that there are some parts of the experience that could've been better and less frustrating.

[h1] The Good [/h1] 

The gameplay loop is very engaging if not addictive. Soundtracks are great, and there are some that I’d definitely want to add to my own library. And it also has a very strong plot filled with well fleshed out characters that you learn more about as you progress through the game.

But I'll focus more on specific gameplay components. As a party-based RPG game, this game did so many things right! First, each character has their own unique mechanic that adds such a depth and uniqueness to each of them. Each of them also has their own skill trees where you can pick their playstyle. Customizing each character and building a team is very satisfying.

One prominent battle mechanic in this game is the time-pressed mechanic, which includes dodging and parrying. Dodging is more error-tolerant, but parrying has big rewards because you gain extra AP (Mana point in this game) and can counterattack with big damage when you do it perfectly. And parrying perfectly is SO SATISFYING. They’re not easy, but it’s part of the charm in the game. I usually don't play souls-like games but this must be how it feels to beat difficult bosses in those games when you learn their attack patterns.

This game did a good job to create hidden corners or optional "bosses” that give you good rewards like items or weapons. This game also doesn’t have random encounters making exploration a smoother experience. Non-random encounters blend well with how tough the enemies are. You get less fights number-wise, but each fight packs more substance. You don’t get full HP recovery but it works out just fine with refillable elixirs and potions. AP also resets for every battle.

All good designs that allow players to pay more attention to individual fights instead of worrying about resource management. Overall, I genuinely had a fantastic time with this game despite some of its flaws that I'll talk about next.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

Now it’s time for me to criticize everyone’s favorite baby in 2025. And there are a few big points not including more minor stuff.

[h2] Main critiques [/h2]

I have 2 main critiques.

The first thing is the clash between parrying (and probably time-pressed mechanics more broadly) with team building and turn-based strategy. While I enjoy team-building and I always customize my team, there are several occasions in the game in which I thought “this feels like I can just parry my way through it.” And I sure did. This means the team-building aspect didn’t get pushed to its full potential because players can just “git gud” to beat certain battles (and some even require it). This creates a divergence in gameplay experience that tries to pull you in 2 different directions. Do you want me to approach it as a strategic turn-based battle or do you want me to engage in this semi-darksouls mechanic where I need to learn the rhythm of the enemies’ attacks?

But the bigger issue of the two I have is that their open world is highly unbalanced or too open, and this becomes very apparent in the 3rd act. This was exacerbated by the previous problem because you could parry your way through optional bosses and end up over-leveling your team for the story. Specifically, the first glaring encounter of this experience for me was me beating Chromatic Chapelier. After that fight, I was practically bullying the 2 axons. I almost had no need to parry or dodge any attack to win them, it was that EASY. And in the 3rd act, you suddenly get inundated with so many side dungeons and bosses you don’t even know where to begin. But because of their “let’s the player ♥♥♥♥ around and find out”, I could easily run into a high level dungeon, end up beating it, and flattening the difficulty of the rest of the content. And that did happen… The final boss fight of the main story can’t even be called a battle for me. There was not a single attack from the boss because I finished it off before that even happened… It ruined the experience of this supposedly difficult game for me. This could’ve easily been solved by adding a “suggested level” indicator to dungeons.

[h2] Medium-level issues [/h2]

These are not the biggest problems in the grand scheme of things, but they did create a moderate level of frustration and dissatisfaction.

First, while it has so much potential for you to customize the characters and create a specific playstyle for them, it’s still lacking in term of team synergy. Specifically, it’s pretty tricky to build playstyle of party members that bounce combo with one another. One part is there’s not enough shared mechanics / resources for characters to combo on. The only obvious two are just Mark and Burn. But that’s it. But it’s also worsened by the fact that this game has a few too many components. To re-customize a build of a character, you need to adjust their weapon, stats, skills, pictos, and lumina. Five separate components is a lot. It’s a barrier to re-customization if you want to change a character’s playstyle, and you have to do this for 2-3 characters to create a balanced party.

Second, lack of (mini-)maps in dungeons. Like I get it, you want us to get lost and be immersed in these dungeons and giant-ass environment. But I was not having it. I generally find a lot of 3D environment to be overwhelming to begin with, and this is exacerbated by the fact that many regions of dungeons are not visually differentiable. There were way too many times where I had to walk through the same route again just to make sure I’ve explored it already. And this may be just minor inconvenience at first. The thing that pushed this problem into a medium-level issue is the fact that at a certain point in the game, you unlocked an ability to break through inaccessible areas that you’ve run into before in previous dungeons (though they’re optional)… I don’t know about everyone, but I shall not be re-traversing those dungeons just to find those hidden areas that I can now access specifically because they don’t have maps!

Third, the pacing… While if you only look at the main story, they’re well-paced enough. But once you consider how many side dungeons and side bosses there are to explore and fight, it clashes with the narrative of “urgency” in the game. Lune literally said “we have no time for detour” and repeat some variants of this many times. And I was like “we had detoured plenty.” It’s not the biggest issue for me, but it’s worth acknowledging.

[h2] Minor problems [/h2]

Now I have a lot of minor complaints, so I’m just gonna list them down very briefly
[list]
    [*]This game could do without platforming. Seriously, it has no business here.
    [*]Verso’s Draft is not all that fun.
    [*]Weapon leveling feel a bit unpredictable sometimes (probably because of monster drop) and detracts a bit from player's choice freedom.
    [*]Honestly, maybe too many items? At a certain point, I gave up mastering all lumina.
[/list]

compact, atmospheric adventure that trades spectacle for slow‑burn tension and careful observation; it’s a game that asks you to move deliberately, listen closely, and let small discoveries accumulate into a larger, unsettling picture. The visual design is the first thing that lingers: muted palettes, careful use of shadow, and restrained lighting create a world that feels half‑remembered and slightly off‑kilter, where every corridor and ruined module reads like a page from a faded field journal. That aesthetic isn’t just pretty it’s functional, guiding your eye toward clues and making environmental storytelling do the heavy lifting. Gameplay is built around exploration and puzzle solving with a focus on inventory‑light mechanics and environmental interaction; puzzles are rarely obtuse and usually reward patience and attention rather than trial‑and‑error, and the pacing gives those moments of revelation room to breathe. Sound design and ambient detail amplify the unease: distant creaks, the hiss of failing systems, and sparse musical cues turn empty spaces into places that feel inhabited by memory. The narrative unfolds in fragments, leaning on implication and mood rather than explicit exposition, which will delight players who enjoy piecing together lore from scraps but may frustrate those who want a more direct story. Technically the game is tidy controls are responsive and the UI keeps the focus on exploration — though a few rough edges in camera framing and checkpoint spacing can interrupt the flow on occasion. Overall Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is a thoughtful, well‑crafted indie experience for players who prefer atmosphere, careful design, and slow‑burn mystery over loud action; it’s the kind of game you play when you want to be quietly unsettled and rewarded for paying attention.

I think this has to be the best game ever made. There are very few things to dislike about the game.

-- The positive
Story: 9.5/10: The story is phenomenal, the foreshadowing is on point enough that you can guess what is to come, but it develops in a way interesting enough that you will not get it quite right.
Graphics: 9/10: The graphics and environments are some of the most beautiful I have ever seen. Some very minor stuttering occured every now and then, but for the rest the game ran smoothly.
Music: 10/10 - The music is what brings most of the emotions to the storytelling for me and is what will bring you from screaming with joy and feeling amazing after a boss fight to crying just minutes after.
Gameplay: 9/10 - The gameplay is an innovative take on a jrpg, especially on a higher difficulty it feels like a combination of a jrpg and dark souls.
Stability: 10/10 - I encountered not a single bug or crash during my 55 hour playthrough. The only thing that could be perceived a a bug is the camera spawning in an odd angle.

-- The negative
Something that made the combat in this game as phenomenal as it is is the combination of the very clear animations and sound design, allowing the player to consistently parry almost everything. In act3 this all goes out the window. The sound design for the parry is slightly off on several monsters, which means a skill you have been training consistently makes you miss your parries now. Additionally they seem to play with the animation sliders, slowing up and speeding down at very weird unintuitive moments, making the parries even harder. This resulted in a rather frustrating act 3 that I only kept going through because I wanted to see if my guesses about the story were correct.

What made this even more jarring is that the execution on animations and sound throughout the rest of the game is phenomenally well done.

One other thing I kind of disliked is that there seems to be a lot of 'post-game' content that you get exposed to throughout the story, but only really explore at the very end of the game as optional content. I can see that this is fun for RPG completionists, but honestly those areas felt a little misplaced to me.

Overall this is the best game ever made and you should play it.

Why do I even need to leave a positive review for almost a 1.5 year old game with already overwhelmingly positive reviews?
- For those who come after.

[h3]Story - 10/10[/h3]
Just... experience it yourself, really. And avoid ANY spoilers. This game will repeatedly subvert your expectations, surprise you, make you smile, make you cry, make you feel excited and determined to change the fate itself in one moment, and then utterly helpless and broken the next. Live through it yourself. Meet it's characters. Saying goodbye to them at the end might prove harder than it seems.
One important note I have to make, though - it is a linear story. Your choices matter little, there are two endings and you choose which one you want manually. The only RPG elements are builds, progression and excellent story. But you don't really get to roleplay; just immerse in the story you follow through the protagonist's eyes.

[h3]Gameplay - 7/10[/h3]
It's not for everyone. It is a JRPG formula (like older Final Fantasy games), with turn based combat and party system. The only major difference is the rhythm-based defensive mechanics. You don't just tank the incoming attacks - you're supposed to dodge and/or parry them, like it's some soulslike. It CAN be annoying. It CAN be tedious. But it does get better, it has a lot of potential for different builds and the ability to create something incredibly OP with the right skills and gear. But what truly matters is that for it's story - those caveats can be ignored.

[h3]Graphics - 7.5/10[/h3]
From technical standpoint, it's nothing mind-blowing with the exception of motion capture in cutscenes (just cutscenes; the in-game facial animations are just okay) - those are spectacular. The textures can be a bit low res at places, some spots do feel like just royalty free assets thrown in together in a messy, yet stylish manner. But the overall art style is great. It works, it works exceptionally well for it's intended purpose. Once you realize what the world you're traveling through really IS... it will all click.

[h3]Sound - 10/10[/h3]
Voice acting remains amazing throughout the whole game. Soundtrack is something one couldn't possibly expect to be made by a relatively rookie composer. And yet it was. And it is nothing short of a masterpiece. Just... be sure not to listen too much to it's lyrics if you know French (especially archaic French) well - it does tend to spoil a lot of the story twists waaaaay ahead them actually happening, lol.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
9/10. It's one of the few titles who claimed the GOTY and actually earned it. The only title they received that, in my opinion, they didn't deserve, is the RPG of the year. This title rightfully belongs to KCD2.

Aesthetically, it's a really impressive effort for such a small studio.  The world looks appropriately fractured, painterly, and dreamlike. Cut scenes are well-rendered, with natural and expressive animations. The soundtrack is serviceable--but I'm a little baffled by folks claiming it's the best thing ever, but you really can't go wrong with classically-inspired themes and angelic choirs.

The plot I can't speak much for because I won't make it through to the end of the game. It started off with a fascinating, rich concept that had me hooked hard at the very beginning, with strong themes of grief, acceptance and persistence in the face of a cruel and uncaring universe. Since then, the storytelling has fallen off pretty hard.  The story is conveyed almost entirely through dialogue and cutscenes, which are loaded with really lackluster g-rated banter, and entire conversations that convey no information because the writers are just desperate to be mysterious.  The characters are all distinct, believable people (the ones that are people, anyway) with personalities ranging from 'likable but forgettable' all the way down to 'shut up shut up shut up shut up.'  The latter happens mostly because the writers try and fail to be funny.  The acting, however, is absolutely stellar on every level.

So, if this game was a film, and had to stand on artistic merits alone, it would be a very solid recommendation--not really in a league with the best, but absolutely worth a playthrough.

The problem is. It's a video game.  And the gameplay is awful.

Let's start with the exploration. Each area is given a distinctive visual design, but once you're in that area it's a bunch of same-looking tunnels with no landmarks or minimap to help with navigation, and nothing interesting to stumble across when you inevitably wander around lost.  Around every corner, there's a fight--usually with the same small handful of enemies you've been fighting every couple of minutes (or couple of seconds) for the past hour-so getting anywhere feels like a complete slog. 

 And to be honest there just isn't much of interest to find out there.  I would have thought that a game that so heavily emphasized this idea of legacy--67 whole expeditions giving their lives to pave their way "for those who come after"--you would actually get to spend more time following in the previous expeditions' footsteps, searching for clues, learning their story and piecing together their knowledge.. but anything of that nature is reserved for cutscenes.  In exploration, the most you'll find of previous expeditions is their old campsites and some one-page journals that tell you absolutely nothing.  Instead, you walk a few feet, fight something, grab generic loot, rinse and repeat while your sense of curiosity withers and dies.

And then there is the other thing. The combat.  The game's core concept is to incorporate mechanically-demanding dodge-parry mechanics into a turn-based combat system. I've seen the idea work in a few other games.  But here, it's actually really awful.  The game is desperately trying to be a soulslike JPRPG, but I'm sorry--there's nothing fun about a soulslike where your feet are nailed to the ground and you're constantly flipping through menus.  Nor do I care for a JRPG where strategy comes secondary to raw mechanical input.

 Parry counterattacks are implemented in such a way that, while they are pretty obnoxious to pull off (the visual indicators are so inconsistent that it's sometimes [i]easier[/i] to parry if you don't look at your screen at all, and rely exclusively on audio queues) but they're also overbalanced as hell.  If you don't parry, you die.  And if you do parry, you take no damage, you [i]deal[/i] massive damage, and you recharge your resources.  It's so strong that every other combat mechanic in the game becomes irrelevant--you can skip all your turns, only parry, and still win the majority of battles.  And frankly most of the combat encounters don't have interesting mechanics to them at all, other than increasingly ridiculous (I've heard up to 20 consecutive parries in late-game) parry combos, and parrying increasingly weird, gimmicky fakeouts.

Learning to consistently land parries in the first few hours of gameplay was fun, and was satisfying for a few more hours after that but halfway through the first act it had already become [i]boring.[/i] And that would have been fine, really, if the gameplay didn't revolve almost entirely around slogging through one fight after another just to be drip-fed fragments of story every couple of hours.  I kept slogging through the rest of the first act, hoping things would start to click, or maybe the story would get good enough to warrant the slog, but... really I just got to the point where I had no desire to boot this game up again.

The combat is built around you mastering the timing of four different kinds of "press this button at the right time" mechanics - which at first seems fun and refreshing. But they take it a little too far.  Every enemy will go out of its way to juke you, fake you out, and generally try to trick you into doing it too early or too late - and after a while you will inevitably picture a smug, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chainsmoking cigarettes in a beret developer going "honhonhonhon je sui so clevér! It sounds like something ridiculous to complain about but after hours of it it just really started to make the experience drag. So yeah, fair warning, if you don't like that, what would otherwise have been a flawless experience will become a trudge. In fairness, the game is very forgiving - you can retry any and every fight if you lose without losing any progress or choose to go back to just before the fight (losing at most minutes of trekking) if you feel you lost due to being underleveled/etc. It's just really obnoxious about it all....

Well, I can't believe I'm actually playing this game because I've largely put it off due to the crazy amount of hype and bandwagon-ing surrounding it, but 10 hours into the expedition I do have to say, the game managed to deliver my expectations and some. I don't know if I would necessarily rank E33 along the all-time greatest titles, but it definitely shows that it is made with love and care, something that is exceedingly rare in today's gaming market.

The game has absolutely phenomenal visual presentation, and supports the ultrawide format natively. I've ran the game on both 4K 32" and 1440p 34" ultrawide, and in both instances the game looks beautiful but for this kind of story-driven adventure, I do personally prefer the ultrawide form factor for its immersion. There was only one time where the game had a very brief black boxes around the sides during Maelle's Nightmare, but otherwise so far everything ran natively 21:9 no issues.

As someone who hated games that every single person talks about over and over, and being a rather harsh critic having grown up on titles like Chrono Trigger, Skyrim, Diablo, Warcraft and other all-time classics, E33 did manage to win me over. Whether it be the art direction, soundtrack, character design, storytelling or combat, it passes everything I have hoped that it would given its reputation. 

The operatic soundtrack sets the tone immediately and the amount of variation played on the main motif is refreshing and artistically delivered. In E33, music is not only integral to the experience but builds upon the narrative being driven, adding suspense, tenderness and other mixes of emotions during key moments of battle and story reveals. The pacing is very solid, there is just the right amount of storytelling mixed in with going through dungeons, and truly there's just never a dull moment unless you specifically choose to venture off into the wild and do the side content. The optional content gives nice outfits and weren't just entirely braindead "go fetch X item to Y" entirely, it feels like even the side NPCs serve some level of purpose instead of just being there for the sake of being there. 

I think most players will be pulled into the story 1-2 hours in and continue onwards seeking to find out more. This is exactly what happened to me and when a game manages to captivate, that's really all there needs to be said at the end of the day. I felt connected to the characters and shared their sense of hopelessness, dread, fear and desire to push on, it didn't feel like another cheap iteration of "random gang of nobodies goes out to fight big evil thing and save the world from certain doom" even though I do believe that's the idea so far, but perhaps I will have to revisit this point once I'm fully finished with the game. 

Just a quick final note for an initial impression, combat is very satisfying and I love that the game offers you rewards for playing well. If you learn the attacking patterns of enemies and can reliably parry/counter, you are able to take on enemies that if you were just playing a plain turn-based combat RPG you wouldn't be able to. Challenging the player to play well and rewarding them for it is an excellent approach to combat that I wish more games would adopt instead of just letting you grind mindlessly, get overlevelled and spam the A button to victory. You can do that too in E33, if you so wish, but that does take away the satisfaction of taking down a big baddie that you know you otherwise shouldn't have been able to if you didn't play very well and parried attacks on-point. The sound effects when you do land a counter also just gives such a nice dopamine hit, you love to see and hear it.

So far, there's really nothing negative I can pick out about E33 and I hope this will continue to be the case when I've completed my first run.

## Why

- JRPG combat for a souls-like fan
- Incredible, emotional story
- Voice actors live up to their reputations and the composer earned one
- I've never taken more screenshots in a game
- Somehow walks the tightrope of funny/traumatic

## Why Not

- You hate games?
- You only have a Steam Deck :/

## Impressions

Some games are so hyped it seems impossible for them to ever meet those expectations. Most don't, especially in the AAA space. I'm pleased to report Expedition 33 is not one of those, instead joining the Silksong pantheon of games you've been endlessly told are the best thing you'll ever play then turn out to be _better_.

To be fair, Clair Obscur may as well as well have been grown in a lab to appeal specifically to me. It takes the turn based, unbelievably stylish but ultimately unengaging combat of Persona 5 Royal and adds... quick time events. Not the most original idea, Paper Mario did it long ago as did plenty of copycats. What sets these particular quick time events apart is the sheer _impact_ of them, and tying the defensive ones to enemy animations rather than flashing button prompts.

Right from the tutorial you can dodge attacks with a well timed button press, or parry them with tighter timing to gain energy for your skills and trigger a high-damage counterattack if you parry every attack in the chain. As if the gameplay rewards weren't enough to encourage parrying it's further promoted by how much better it feels through sound design and animation, peaking when you nail every attack in the chain and annihilate the enemy with damage than you otherwise could do in several turns (at least early game). This burst of damage, coupled with complete damage negation on successful parries and dodges, leads to the other inspiration for the Expedition's brilliant combat; Elden Ring.

Just like any good souls-like, if you learn their patterns well enough Clair Obscur's toughest enemies will fall even if you're well below the recommended level. This more or less eliminates any need for typical JRPG grinding; just following the main story will give you enough levels to take down bosses in a reasonable time. Enemies also don't just scale their numbers, they scale in attack pattern complexity (as well as introducing two new counters for different situations) and gimmicks to solve.

Something like an SL1 run probably isn't feasible; this is a JRPG after all. One notorious lategame boss has 50 million health; that'd probably be a multi-week ordeal of perfect parries with your paltry level one damage. But in more realistic scenarios you're unlikely to struggle; I followed the main story to exclusion of all side content up until the end of Act 1 and despite feeling challenged never struggled unduly.

Which is good, because the main story is really tough to set aside. The characters carry it, thanks to strong writing an predictably fantastic performances from a star-studded voice cast, but the overall plot is also strong and packed with twisty mystery. As expected of a world whose premise is a yearly culling of every human above a certain age, the story is pretty damn dark. However the writers managed to find plenty of opportunities to inject just the right amount of levity and silliness, keeping things from getting unbearably heavy. I won't go into details on the story because if you've somehow managed to avoid spoilers like I did you're in for a treat; suffice to say I'll think back to this game plenty over the years to come.

In conclusion Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 absolutely deserves all the accolades and praise which have been heaped upon it. If you like JRPGs, souls-likes, good stories or just games in general you absolutely need to play it. Fantastic work to the team at Sandfall, the voice actors and the composer; can't wait to see what they cook up next.

I only review games I've 100%.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has one of the best stories I've played in years. The pacing is incredibly tight, the twists genuinely land, and the use of mocap, real faces, and phenomenal voice acting makes every scene feel unusually human. The characters are lovable, the themes are beautifully handled, and Ben Starr and Renoir's VA are especially incredible.

The soundtrack might be my favorite ever. It's classical, dramatic, emotional, and feels meticulously written around every scene. Understanding the French lyrics made it hit even harder. Robe de Jour has been permanently stuck in my head.

The UI and RPG systems are more mixed. Pictos and Luminas are fun to experiment with, but unlocking them through repeated battles feels like unnecessary busywork. The UI also feels oversized and slightly messy for a game where you spend so much time navigating menus.

My biggest issue by far is the difficulty design. Normal combat is fantastic. Parries, breaks, counters, huge damage numbers, all incredibly satisfying. But harder encounters often devolve into enemies one-shotting your entire party through absurd multi-hit combos that you basically have to memorize and perfectly parry. It stopped feeling challenging and started feeling tedious, to the point where I just built around one-shotting bosses instead.

Performance was also awful for me. On an RTX 5070 I dealt with constant frame drops, GPU crashes, and eventually DX12 stopped launching entirely, forcing me onto DX11. I even fought one late-game boss at around 15 FPS.

The completionist experience was actually one of the better parts. It pushed me into side content I probably would've skipped otherwise, and a surprising amount of it meaningfully expands the lore and strengthens the story even further. Hidden bosses and collectibles kept it engaging without becoming an insane grind, and I really appreciated not being forced into NG+ outside of a few missables.

Those gripes really hurt because underneath the balance and performance problems is a game I otherwise would've considered a masterpiece. Sadly, they soured the experience enough that I can't.
