I really only recommend this game for the gameplay, not for the story, which I'll get into later. I will avoid spoilers entirely, only abbreviating or loosely referencing elements.

It's admittedly short for an narrative JRPG-styled game, with my first playthrough clocking in around 30 hours, and I think that boils down to the fact that it's fairly (not fully) linear until late in. Side quests, more towns and NPC stories, and even something as simple as inventory management would have added a lot of time and enjoyment into my camp, personally.

The combat is stellar. The mix of souls-like and traditional turn-based RPG are very refreshing. Exploring areas feels good, and finding secrets is fairly rewarding. The sheer expansiveness of the skill system is to be applauded, you can do a LOT with builds, despite the limited cast. Some characters are callbacks to classic RPG with a new twist, such as the "blue mage" with the rotating combat wheel.

I look forward to this team's next project with a bit more time and budget behind them. Having something like a bestiary, side quests, and overall more information about the world as we discover more of it would be a masterwork, I think.

The negatives of the gameplay are fairly simple: "S" is a fight with a fairly nonsensical bit of artificial difficulty strapped on that's really just a party check that kind of ruins the fun of their parry mechanics, taking a cool and satisfying to fight super-boss and turning it into one of my least favorite fights. The platforming should not exist in a game with an auto-roll and floaty baby-jumps. Falling through random rocks and getting stuck because the designers decided not to go through the areas and smooth out the terrain can also be frustrating at times. That's really about it.
(Edited note: I must say that my negatives from a gameplay perspective are all optional content and will not impact how you enjoy the game unless you choose to let them impact you.)

The story: 

TLDR: Maelle's narrative is lovely. The male leads are incredibly shallow and ruin the story for me.

Extended: It's not by any means the second-coming of RPG Jesus that everyone led me to believe. This is why hype kills narrative games: It's all subjective. In my eyes, Expedition 33 is very much a - and I hate to say the word - Mary-Sue focused narrative about a bunch of men who suspiciously look like the CEO; The man who is also the writer and creative lead of the project. 

A huge sour point for me is how they pull the trigger on what could be a very intense moment far too early, and instantly fill the void with more of the same. That's about as much as I can say about that without spoiling anything. Maelle's story is lovely, and I enjoyed that aspect greatly, but every moment spent there was a reminder of the personality black-holes that are the male leads.

I also feel that the camp scenes should have been more frequent, and less cut off. It felt like the moment a scene was getting interesting, it faded to black and told me what cool things were happening between the characters, rather than letting me hear the dialog and be a part of the character bonding; Letting me get attached to these lovingly crafted characters.

That all said, Esquie is a treasure and I would protect them forever, and I still fully recommend the game to anyone who wants a linear narrative experience with great gameplay.

I had no expectations when I saw this title pop up in reviews, awards, 'before you buy', instagram shorts of streamers who became emotional in some parts of the story. So it piqued my interest. But after going midway through the story, I can finally say I have had enough and I do not recommend it. So dear devs and fellow players, buckle up and check out this point of view:

There are a lot of good remarks to be made, some given the fact that this was a game made by a small studio and others because the devs really tried to push the boundaries of what's acceptable in a modern title and what would the players enjoy. But any positive thing I will list below is getting crushed by the horrible mix of gameplay elements, making the gameplay itself the least favorable element of the game, and also the reason why I don't even want to finish the story anymore.

On the pros:
-Outstanding art direction, vibrant colors and lush environments fill the screen at any moment
-Memorable characters with natural development through their interactions with one another and the world
-No words needed for the music, soundtracks are made with passion and each convey a feeling
-Interesting enemy art and unique creatures
-A plus for every playable character as they have a unique style and abilities to choose from
-It runs buttery smooth on Epic with RT on and all, but this is subjective as I made my PC to run the UE5 editor heavy projects

Now for the cons:
-The topmost issue with the game, the gameplay. It starts with challenge and mystery, then you get to unlock abilities, you learn how to heal, defend your party etc etc. So the difficulty curve is well designed. But then, the parry mechanic comes into place. First it seems optional but later on, every fight becomes a parry-race. You learn more parrying techniques. Then how to chain parries or parry counter attacks on top of your attacks. Then, skills, abilities, strategy, are all thrown to the bin because you have to parry every single encounter and attack. There is also the option to dodge, but doesn't give anything back, so you don't have AP to play.
-Platforming. There are weirdly placed platforming sections, some of them unbalanced even that don't match the rest of the game.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Is a Masterpiece That Redefines What Games Can Be

Every once in a generation, a game comes along that reminds us why we fell in love with gaming in the first place. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is that game.

Calling it "excellent" feels inadequate. Calling it a "masterpiece" somehow undersells what Sandfall Interactive has achieved. This isn't just one of the best RPGs of recent years it's the kind of experience that makes you question whether other games have been trying hard enough.

From the moment the first notes of the soundtrack begin to play, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 grabs hold of your soul and refuses to let go. Its world is breathtakingly beautiful, blending dark fantasy, surrealism, and Belle Époque inspired artistry into something that feels completely unique. Every environment looks like a painting that somehow came to life. Every scene could be framed and hung in a museum.

Then there's the story.

Most games tell a story. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 delivers an emotional assault. It doesn't simply entertain—it devastates, inspires, and lingers in your mind long after the credits roll. The characters aren't just companions; they become people you genuinely care about. Their struggles, hopes, and sacrifices hit with a force rarely seen in any medium, let alone video games.

And the combat? Somehow, it manages to take the best elements of classic turn-based RPGs and inject them with enough adrenaline to make your heart race. Every battle feels meaningful. Every dodge, parry, and perfectly timed counterattack transforms encounters into a thrilling dance between strategy and skill. It's as if someone took the tactical brilliance of the greatest JRPGs ever made and fused it with the intensity of an action game.

The soundtrack deserves its own standing ovation. It doesn't accompany the experience—it elevates it. Every track feels handcrafted to maximize emotion, whether you're exploring a mysterious landscape, facing impossible odds, or witnessing a heartbreaking story moment. There are songs here that deserve to be remembered among the greatest pieces of music ever written for a video game.

What's most astonishing is that this comes from a relatively new studio. Many AAA developers with budgets ten times larger would struggle to create something with even half the creativity, passion, and artistic vision on display here. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 feels like a game created by people who genuinely love the medium and wanted to prove that video games can still surprise us.

This is not merely a Game of the Year contender. It's a once-in-a-decade RPG. It's the kind of title people will reference years from now when discussing the greatest games of its era. It's the reason people buy gaming hardware. It's the game you'll recommend to friends, strangers, family members, and probably your mail carrier.

If you have even the slightest appreciation for storytelling, music, world-building, art direction, or RPG combat, you owe it to yourself to experience Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.

This is possibly one of the best games to come out in the last 10 years.

That’s quite a bold statement, but for me, this game deserves all the praise it’s getting.

The story is simply superb. You get hooked within the first 10–15 minutes. The writing is amazing, and the world-building is coherent, detailed, and incredibly rich.

Gameplay is classic JRPG-style turn-based combat with some nice twists that keep you engaged at all times. Even on the hardest difficulty, it’s quite manageable for most of the game, but towards the end, you really need to master the build system and all the battle mechanics to be able to defeat the extra final bosses.

And the graphics… this game is absolutely gorgeous. It’s a game you really want to experience in the highest quality possible.

The soundtrack is also something special that I still find myself listening to in my day-to-day life. Sound effects are on point.

Even after getting all the achievements, I still wanted to 100% it and check out all the extra fights, items, lore, and cutscenes. That’s how much the game kept me engaged.

Regarding negative points, there are a few, but they are mostly nitpicks. Some cutscene animations, particularly eye positioning, can feel slightly off and take away a bit of immersion. I also notice some reused running animations between characters (for example, a male character using the same running animation as a female one).

Nevertheless, it was a privilege to experience this game :)

I finished my first playthrough recently, and honestly, I didn’t expect to get this invested in the game. I knew it was good, but I didn’t expect to become this immersed in the world and characters, especially considering that I normally don’t care much about turn-based games. The combat completely won me over, mainly because of the parry and dodge mechanics. They make it much more interactive than a traditional turn-based system, and as someone who really likes Sekiro and Souls-like games, it clicked with me immediately. You’re not just sitting there waiting for your turn, you actually have to pay attention and react to what the enemy is doing. The build system is also really fun once you understand how everything works, and by the end I was having a great time experimenting with different builds. I played on Expert and found the difficulty pretty well balanced. At first I expected it to be much harder, but eventually I actually started feeling overpowered once I figured out the systems.

The story is probably my favorite part. It hooked me almost immediately and made me genuinely care about what would happen to the characters. Maelle, Verso, Renoir and Simon were probably my favorites, with Renoir being the one I liked the most story-wise. The game is also insanely cinematic. Some of the cutscenes genuinely felt like I was watching a movie, and the presentation is just fantastic overall. I went with [spoiler] Verso’s [/spoiler] ending on my first playthrough and really liked it. I also checked out the other ending afterwards, but personally I think [spoiler] Verso’s [/spoiler] is better and feels more mature. The visuals are another huge highlight. I’m normally not someone who takes many screenshots, but I couldn’t stop myself here. And somehow, despite how good everything looks, the game is also really well optimized. I played for around 120 hours and didn’t encounter a single bug. Considering that this was made by a relatively small team and is essentially their first game of this scale, that’s honestly crazy. Winning GOTY 2025 feels completely deserved to me.

Of course, it’s not perfect. Some bosses were just not my thing. Chromatic Lampmaster has way too much HP and I absolutely hated the lamp mechanic, while Osquio had the Barbapapa mechanic and took me around 20 minutes to kill. Maybe I was underleveled, so I’m not completely sure about the HP, but that was way too long for me. I’m also not a fan of bosses that spend most of the fight summoning other enemies, which is why Clea and Clea Unleashed didn’t really click with me either, although I liked those fights much more from a lore perspective. I also think the semi-open-world approach was a bit of a mistake. There aren’t that many meaningful optional locations, and some places basically exist just to give you a music record. The flying ability comes pretty late too, despite making travelling around the world much more convenient. Personally, I think the game would have been better as a more linear experience with larger and more interconnected areas, something closer to DS3 or BB.

The 9,999 damage cap before [spoiler] killing the Paintress [/spoiler] is another thing I really disliked. I understand why they needed some way to stop players from becoming ridiculously strong too early, but I think there were better solutions. They could have spread the strongest Pictos throughout the later parts of the game or simply made the cap much higher and balanced boss HP around it. Reaching 9,999 damage is actually pretty easy once you understand the build system, so the cap ends up limiting build variety more than I think it should. The side quests are also pretty forgettable, but honestly, that didn’t bother me too much because the main story and characters are much more important to me.

Despite all of that, I had an amazing time with it. It managed to make me enjoy a genre I normally have almost no interest in, and that alone says a lot. The combat feels great, the story kept me invested, the characters are memorable, the soundtrack and visuals are fantastic, and the whole thing has an atmosphere that really pulled me in. Seeing what such a relatively small team managed to accomplish with essentially their first game of this scale makes it even more impressive. There are definitely things I’d like to see them improve in their next game, especially the world design, some boss mechanics and the damage progression, but the foundation is already incredibly strong.

For me, it’s a solid 9/10.
